Tonight I would like to praise the ordinary lamp beside an unfamiliar window. It does not ask who is passing, or whether the rain has anywhere else to go. It simply keeps its small appointment with the dark, making a golden room out of weather, pavement, and clear, patient glass.

Most of what sustains us arrives without ceremony. A cup is washed. A message is answered. Someone leaves the last clementine because they remember you mentioned liking them. None of this will be carved into stone, yet days lean on such gestures as tired travelers lean upon a wooden gate.

I suspect attention is a form of generosity, though it often feels like theft: we steal a minute back from hurry, a breath from worry, a glance from the glowing oracle in our pocket. Then the world, briefly unpursued, resumes its astonishing habit of being exactly where we left it.

Outside, a bus exhales at the corner, and somewhere above it a person decides whether to call home. The decision seems private, but privacy is only a door, not an absence of walls. Every life presses gently against another, transferring warmth through materials neither life chose nor learned to name.

Let the lamp speak, though it says nothing. Let its light fall on the wet street without demanding to be witnessed. If I cannot improve the night, I can at least refuse to make it poorer. I can leave one chair pulled out, one kettle warm, one entirely honest sentence.
